title: A Weather for the Radiators
premise: Coral Eriksen has spent eleven years as a bridge inspector and a quiet wife, cataloguing cracks in steel and in her marriage to Hal, whose family has never explained why his brother Danny vanished after a fire in their old neighborhood. When a late-night radio station plays a song Danny wrote and never recorded—sung by a voice Coral recognizes as Hal's—she realizes the family's tidy story of disappearance was a shared fiction, arranged around a night someone in the family committed a crime the law never caught. Following the song's broadcast backwards through rerouted bus lines, aging witnesses, and her own unreliable memories of her wedding day, Coral forces each Eriksen to choose between loyalty and truth. In the end she testifies to what she saw as a bride, sending her brother-in-law's protector—her own mother-in-law—to face a court that can finally act, and leaves the marriage not in bitterness but in ownership of her own life.
about_author: Vesper Fairweather is the pen name of a former municipal engineer who spent a decade inspecting bridges in the industrial Midwest before turning to fiction. Her work examines the quiet architectures of family loyalty, and she still cannot hear a radio without checking the frequency twice.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Coral, in her own POV, inspects a decaying drawbridge while mentally measuring her marriage's tolerances—Hal's silences, the family dinners she endures as a tenant. A routine call about rerouting the old 42 bus line to the Eriksens' former neighborhood unsettles her. Emotional beat: numb competence cracking into vague dread.

chapters.title: A Song Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Driving home at 2 a.m., Coral hears a late-night radio program play a song she once heard Danny Eriksen sing privately at her wedding rehearsal—written, never recorded, never performed since. The DJ says the tape arrived anonymously. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past announcing itself in the present tense.

chapters.title: The Family Arrangement
chapters.summary: At Sunday dinner, Coral watches Hal, his mother Ruth, and sister June perform normalcy, testing them with oblique questions about Danny. Each deflects with rehearsed ease, revealing the family's choreography around his absence. POV: Coral, with a flashback section in Hal's voice. Emotional beat: the realization that silence is a group project.

chapters.title: What the Bride Saw
chapters.summary: Coral excavates her memory of her wedding day, when a drunk Danny pulled her aside and said, 'You'll keep it too, now.' She recalls a figure leaving the old Eriksen house the night of the fire—a figure she agreed, without knowing why, to forget. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: guilt surfacing like rust through paint.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: Coral rides the last weeks of the old 42 route, finding former neighbors: a retired dispatcher who kept a logbook, a shopkeeper who saw who bought accelerant. Each account contradicts the family's version slightly, and each person admits Ruth asked them to let it go. POV: Coral. Emotional beat: the law's failure making her the only available court.

chapters.title: June's Ledger
chapters.summary: June, in her POV, confronts Coral: she has kept a private ledger of the family's lies for twenty years but never acted, believing exposure would kill Ruth. The two women form an uneasy alliance. Emotional beat: loyalty examined and found to be a form of complicity.

chapters.title: The Voice on the Tape
chapters.summary: Hal, in his POV, confesses to the reader he sent the tape: he has sung Danny's song at open mics for years, unable to stop, and mailed it in a moment of self-betrayal. He knows what Ruth did to protect Danny—and what Danny did. Emotional beat: a marriage's two invisibles recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Ruth, Holding
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV: the fire, Danny's panic, her decision to bury it—she has carried the truth so long it has become her spine. She confronts Coral, offering the family's oldest bargain: belonging in exchange for silence. Coral refuses. Emotional beat: love and blackmail revealed as the same gesture.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax. Coral gives a formal statement to a cold-case detective; June corroborates with her ledger; Hal signs an affidavit admitting he helped move evidence as a teenager. Ruth, rather than flee, walks into the station herself, saying she has been waiting for someone to ask. POV: alternating Coral and Ruth. Emotional beat: truth spoken aloud at last, at maximum cost.

chapters.title: A Weather for the Radiators
chapters.summary: Months later: Ruth awaits sentencing with unexpected peace; Danny, found alive and diminished, refuses contact; the 42 line runs its new route past a bridge Coral certified safe. Coral and Hal divorce gently, and she signs the deed to her own apartment—owner, not tenant. She leaves the radio on. Emotional beat: cold clarity, and warmth anyway.
